label: Pre-Transfusion Safety: Human Error at the Bedside (Lecture 21)
rows: Almost universally CLERICAL: the blood bank typed correctly, the unit reached the wrong patient (mislabeled sample, "wrong blood in tube", or a failed two-person bedside check).
Unit for bay 2 given in bay 1 → within 5 minutes rigors, severe flank pain, tachypnea, hypotension, dark port-wine urine.
At the bedside, in front of the patient. Never pre-label; never label away from the patient.
Name, medical record number, unit blood type and unit serial number matched directly against the WRISTBAND.
Infuse the first 25–50 mL slowly: a severe acute hemolytic reaction can follow as little as 25 mL.
No prior verified type on record → a second, separate sample is drawn and tested to confirm ABO/Rh.

label: ABO: Carbohydrate Antigens, Natural IgM, Intravascular Lysis
rows: Oligosaccharides on membrane glycoproteins. Group O = only the unmodified H core. A = N-acetylgalactosamine transferase; B = D-galactosyltransferase; AB = both antigens.
NATURALLY OCCURRING (no transfusion needed), primed in infancy by gut flora and food carbohydrates. You make antibodies against the ABO antigens you lack.
IgM: large pentamer, avid complement fixer (C1q binding).

Membrane attack complex (C5b-9) in the circulation → immediate lysis, free hemoglobin in plasma → C3a and C5a: vasodilation, hypotension, shock → free hemoglobin: tubular precipitation / acute tubular necrosis; procoagulants: disseminated intravascular coagulation.

label: ★ Compatibility Matrix: Red Cells and Plasma Run Opposite

rows.note: Red cells: O = universal donor, AB = universal recipient. Plasma: AB = universal donor (no anti-A or anti-B), O = universal recipient.

mnemonic.hook: "O gives cells, AB gives plasma" — and whoever gives one TAKES the other.
key: gives red cells to all; takes plasma from all
gives plasma to all; takes red cells from all
mnemonic.breaks: Covers the universal rows only. Groups A and B: red cells from their own group or O; plasma from their own group or AB.

label: Emergency Release: O-Negative vs O-Positive
rows: Scarce (~6–7%). Strict reserve: MANDATORY for females of childbearing potential (<50 years) with an unknown type → prevents lifelong anti-D and fetal hydrops in future pregnancies. Sent uncrossmatched while confirmatory testing proceeds.
Abundant (~37–39%). Massive transfusion standard for adult males and post-menopausal females.
NO immediate intravascular hemolysis (no natural anti-D). Anti-D may form later; surviving the hemorrhage comes first.

label: ABO vs RhD Head to Head
rows: Acute, dramatic: shock, acute DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation), acute tubular necrosis
Gradual: asymptomatic hemoglobin drop, mild jaundice (spherocytes, low haptoglobin)

mnemonic.hook: ABO is born with it and bursts cells in the blood; Rh needs a Rehearsal, is Removed by the spleen and Reaches the baby.
mnemonic.breaks: Says nothing about the antigen chemistry (ABO carbohydrate, RhD protein).

label: RhD and Hemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Newborn
rows: Transmembrane protein; the MOST immunogenic red cell antigen outside ABO. Rh-positive = the RhD polypeptide is present.
Rh-negative people have ZERO anti-D at baseline; exposure = Rh-positive transfusion or feto-maternal hemorrhage. Anti-D is IgG (IgG1, IgG3); weeks to months to mature.

RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive fetus → feto-maternal bleed (delivery, trauma) → IgG anti-D → in LATER pregnancies crosses the placenta (Fc receptors) → splenic destruction, anemia, extramedullary hematopoiesis, high-output heart failure (hydrops fetalis).

Masks and clears fetal D-positive cells before maternal B cells respond. ~28 weeks to every non-sensitized RhD-negative mother; within 72 hours of delivering an RhD-positive baby; after miscarriage, ectopic, abortion, amniocentesis or abdominal trauma.
Quantifies the fetal-maternal bleed → are extra vials of Rh immune globulin needed?

label: ★ Reading ABO Typing
cols: Reverse (plasma + A1, B cells): detects ANTIBODIES
rows: Agglutinates both A1 and B cells
No agglutination with anti-A or anti-B

rows.note: Forward and reverse MUST match before blood is released; any discrepancy → immediate investigation.

mnemonic.hook: Forward finds the antigen you HAVE; reverse finds the antibody for what you LACK — so the two halves name the same group from opposite sides.
mnemonic.breaks: Anti-D (Rh) is read only on the forward side.

label: Antibody Screen, DAT vs IAT, Type and Screen vs Crossmatch
rows: An indirect antiglobulin test: plasma + 2–3 group O reagent cells, then antihuman globulin. Finds UNEXPECTED IgG alloantibodies (Kell, Duffy, Kidd, Rh C/E). Negative in ~95–98%.

Alloantibody from prior transfusion, transplantation or pregnancy → 11- to 16-cell identification panel → antigen-negative donor units (hours to days) → order the type and screen well before elective surgery.

"ALREADY coated in the body?" Patient's washed red cells; polyspecific anti-IgG + anti-C3d, then monospecific if positive. Hemolytic reactions, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn.
"FREE antibody in the plasma?" Plasma + reagent cells (in vitro). Pre-transfusion screen, prenatal antibody screen, crossmatching.
ABO, Rh, unexpected antibodies; ZERO units held. Transfusion possible but not expected (routine surgery, stable gastrointestinal bleed).
Physically matches donor units; specific units tagged and RESERVED (unavailable to others until released). Transfusion planned, highly probable or ongoing.
Sample valid only 72 hours if transfused or pregnant within 3 months, or history uncertain: new alloantibodies form fast after re-exposure → expired = redraw and retest.

label: Crossmatch Tiers
rows: Negative screen AND ≥2 concordant type records
Negative screen, no history of significant antibodies
Final ABO check; rules out clerical mismatch
Positive screen OR history of significant antibodies
37 °C + antihuman globulin: weak IgG to minor antigens

key: Electronic: Everything clean (negative screen + two records)
mnemonic.breaks: The letters carry the requirement, not the turnaround times.

label: ★ Any Suspected Reaction: The Universal Response
rows: Halt the infusion immediately; do NOT just slow it. Disconnect the tubing at the catheter hub.
Fresh normal saline through NEW tubing; never flush the remaining blood into the patient.
Wristband vs unit label, bag paperwork and compatibility slip.
Remaining product, intact tubing and tags → blood bank for testing and cultures.
Repeat ABO/Rh, direct antiglobulin test, complete blood count, metabolic panel, free plasma hemoglobin, urinalysis.

label: ★ The Five Reactions: Laboratory Fingerprints
rows: Marked: pink plasma, red urine, low haptoglobin, high LDH
ABO mismatch on recheck; acute DIC
Extravascular: spherocytes, high indirect bilirubin, hemoglobin drop

rows.note: DAT = direct antiglobulin test; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase; DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation; BP = blood pressure. *May be negative if every donor cell is already lysed.

mnemonic.hook: The two A's are Afebrile; the two Hemolytics are DAT-positive.
mnemonic.breaks: The febrile non-hemolytic reaction is the leftover: fever, normal labs, negative DAT. Delayed hemolytic fever is only mild/variable.

label: Reaction by Reaction
rows: ABO (90%+ clerical), IgM + complement, within minutes. Triad: fever/rigors, flank pain, red urine. Labs: absent haptoglobin, very high LDH (lactate dehydrogenase), later indirect bilirubin; DIC labs (long clotting times, high D-dimer, low fibrinogen and platelets); rising creatinine, hyperkalemia.

Anamnestic IgG to minor antigens (Kidd, Rh, Duffy, Kell); old antibody undetectable on the screen. Day 3–30 (peak 5–15). Hemoglobin drops or fails to rise; mild jaundice. New positive DAT + new alloantibody (anti-Jka); spherocytes.
A delayed reaction mimics a pain crisis; hemoglobin A falls disproportionately. Hyperhemolysis: donor AND own cells destroyed, reticulocytopenia, further transfusion can be fatal.

Stored cytokines or anti-white cell (HLA, human leukocyte antigen) antibodies. Rise ≥1 °C to ≥38 °C during or within 4 h; stable. All labs normal. Sepsis workup if ≥2 °C, hypotension or platelets. Prevent: pre-storage leukoreduction; no routine premedication.

Recipient IgE vs donor plasma proteins; plasma-rich products. Hives only: NO fever, wheeze or hypotension; labs normal. Pause, H1-blocker, re-check at 20–30 min → the SAME unit may restart slower within the 4-hour hang time. Wheeze/fever/hypotension → never restart.

Severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA; seconds after 1–5 mL; NO fever (separates it from sepsis and acute hemolysis). Intramuscular epinephrine first, never delayed. Tryptase within 1–3 h, IgA level, anti-IgA. Future: washed red cells or IgA-deficient donors.
